941.quote_or_event: “The union of air, water and fire / the body is the play-thing of the fickle and unsteady intellect.”
941.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak describes the human body as a compound of the elements, air named first, held together for a while and driven about by a restless mind.
941.tie_back: The Kural's physicians count three bodily forces led by wind; Guru Nanak likewise sees the body as a mixture of elements led by air, whose condition depends on how they are held together.
941.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 152, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
941._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse shares the idea of a body made of elements headed by air, but its point is the body's impermanence and the mind's fickleness, not a medical theory of excess and deficiency.

942.quote_or_event: “The Naam is the panacea, the remedy to cure all ills.”
942.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan calls the Name of God the medicine for every ailment, meaning above all the ills of ego, desire and fear that trouble the mind.
942.tie_back: The Kural says that a well-kept regimen makes medicine unnecessary; Gurbani names the one remedy that, practised daily, keeps the inner life from falling sick.
942.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
942._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both speak of a daily discipline that makes other cures unnecessary, but the Kural means diet and the body while Gurbani means spiritual remembrance; Sikhism does not reject ordinary medicine.

943.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you.”
943.explanation: In So Purakh, part of the evening prayer Rehras, Guru Arjan reminds the listener that a human body is a rare gift and the chance it offers should not be wasted.
943.tie_back: The Kural's commentators gloss 'one who has obtained a body' as one granted this hard-won human frame, and urge measured eating so that it lasts; Gurbani shares the sense that the body is a gift to be cared for.
943.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, So Purakh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
943._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse supports the commentators' gloss on the precious human body, but it says nothing about measured eating or long life, and its aim is meeting God rather than physical health.

944.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
944.explanation: In a Sri Raag hymn, Guru Nanak warns against eating for pleasure foods that harm the body and disturb the mind, setting them against the true nourishment of the Name.
944.tie_back: The Kural tells one to keep firmly to foods that agree with the body; Guru Nanak likewise warns against foods that, once eaten, ruin the body.
944.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
944._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on avoiding foods that harm the body, but the hymn adds a moral and spiritual dimension and does not speak of digestion or waiting for real hunger.

945.quote_or_event: “Sleep little, and eat little; O Nanak, this is the essence of wisdom.”
945.explanation: In Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's dialogue with the yogis, this line ends a stanza describing the disciplined seeker who lives in the world without being ruled by appetite.
945.tie_back: The Kural says no harm comes to one who holds back from eating too much even of wholesome food; the verse likewise makes eating little part of wisdom.
945.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 939, Raag Ramkali, Sidh Gosht (pauri 8), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
945._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: translators differ on whether these words describe Guru Nanak's own ideal or the yogis' claim (Manmohan Singh attributes them to the yogis), and Sikhism rejects ascetic fasting, so this is moderation rather than austerity.

946.quote_or_event: “Fareed, my bread is made of wood, and hunger is my appetizer. Those who eat buttered bread, will suffer in terrible pain.”
946.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses the Gurus included in the Granth, contrasts his plain dry bread, made tasty only by hunger, with the rich food of those who indulge and later suffer for it.
946.tie_back: The Kural sets the well-being of the moderate eater against the disease of the glutton; Farid sets plain food eaten in hunger against rich food that brings pain.
946.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 28) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
946._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on plain eating against indulgence; Sikh commentators also read the plain bread as honestly earned and the pain as spiritual as well as bodily.

947.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
947.explanation: Bhagat Kabir names lobh (greed), one of the five thieves of Sikh teaching, as the bringer of death, and sets it against forgiveness.
947.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who thoughtlessly eats beyond measure will suffer diseases beyond measure; Kabir warns more broadly that wherever greed rules, ruin follows.
947.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 155) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
947._accuracy_note: Next-best only: greed is the root of the glutton's excess, but Kabir speaks of greed in general and of spiritual death, not overeating and bodily disease.

948.quote_or_event: “O physician, you are a competent physician, if you first diagnose the disease. Prescribe such a remedy, by which all sorts of illnesses may be cured. Administer that medicine, which will cure the disease, and allow peace to come and dwell in the body.”
948.explanation: In a salok in Guru Nanak's Malaar ki Vaar, Guru Angad addresses the physician: first find the disease, then the remedy, then give the medicine that truly cures.
948.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own three steps: find the disease, find the remedy, then act in the way that fits.
948.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, salok of Guru Angad (Mahala 2) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
948._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the method of diagnosis before treatment; the salok goes on to say the physician must first cure his own disease (ego), so its final aim is spiritual.

949.quote_or_event: “The physician was called in; he touched my arm and felt my pulse. The foolish physician did not know that the pain was in the mind.”
949.explanation: In the salok just before Guru Angad's, Guru Nanak describes a physician who takes the pulse but misses the real illness, the pain of separation from God within.
949.tie_back: The Kural asks the learned physician to weigh the patient's real condition before acting; Guru Nanak shows what goes wrong when a physician does not grasp the patient's true state.
949.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (Mahala 1) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
949._accuracy_note: A strong fit, seen from the other side: the verse warns against misreading the patient, though the hidden illness is spiritual longing and nothing is said of age, strength or season.

950.quote_or_event: During the fighting at Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya, a Sikh of Guru Gobind Singh, carried water to every wounded man, Sikh or enemy. When the Sikh soldiers complained, he told the Guru that he saw no friends or foes, only people, and the Guru is said to have given him medical aid to dress their wounds as well.
950.explanation: Bhai Kanhaiya is remembered as the founder of the Sevapanthi order and as the model of seva to the sick and wounded without distinction.
950.tie_back: The Kural counts the one who stays at the bedside to give the remedy as one of medicine's four parts; Bhai Kanhaiya is the Sikh model of that attendant, with the Guru supplying the remedy.
950.source: Account of Bhai Kanhaiya at Anandpur (c. 1704), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bhai Kanhaiya' (paraphrase)
950._accuracy_note: Partial: the story matches only the attendant and the remedy, not the Kural's full fourfold scheme; it comes from Sikh tradition, and Wikipedia is used here as a last resort for a paraphrase.
